Oxytocin12 and ergot alkaloids13 (usually ergometrine) can both reduce postpar- tum blood loss and appear to be equally effective,12 while the fixed combination Syntometrine (oxytocin and er- gometrine) may be more effective than oxytocin alone in reducing the risk of moderate postpartum haemorrhage (500 to 1000 mL).14 However, ergot alkaloids and Syn- tometrine cause more adverse effects than oxytocin, par- ticularly nausea, vomiting, and raised blood pressure.12,14 Although the quality of evidence is low, WHO recom- mends that oxytocin is generally preferred for prevention of postpartum haemorrhage; an ergot alkaloid (er- gometrine or methylergometrine) or Syntometrine may be used if oxytocin is not available.10 Prostaglandins have also been investigated as an alterna- tive for the routine management of the third stage of la- bour, and there has been particular interest in misoprostol. Although oral or sublingual misoprostol may reduce the risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage (more than 1000 mL), it is less effective than conventional injectable oxytocics.15 Data on other prostaglandins are scarce.15 Based on these findings, a systematic review15 has sug- gested that prostaglandins are not preferrable to oxytocin, but that misoprostol may be used where no injectable oxy- tocic is available. Others have also argued that although misoprostol may be less effective, it would still be useful in developing countries where there are no alternatives,16 and some authorities include misoprostol as an option when other oxytocics are not available or the birth attend- ant’s skills are limited.7,9,10 Where a skilled attendant is not available to provide active management, an appropriately trained healthcare worker may give oxytocin or misoprostol alone for the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage.10 1.
